game: Modern self-explaining management sims: Two Point Hospital, Planet Coaster / Planet Zoo, Parkitect, plus Frostpunk and Anno 1800 notification grammar
core_loop: Moment-to-moment in all of these games: notice a visibly failing agent or building in the world (a queue overflowing a corridor, a red-tinted animal, an "out of stock" sign over a shop, a status icon over an idle factory) -> click the thing itself -> read a small panel that names the cause -> fix it by placing, hiring, or re-routing directly in the world -> watch the flow of bodies/crates/goods resume as confirmation. Session-level: a persistent on-screen objective checklist (star objectives in Two Point Hospital, scenario goals in Parkitect/Planet Zoo career, population tiers in Anno) unlocks a new room/animal/tier, which injects a new visible demand the current lot cannot serve, restarting the loop. Crucially, the reward for fixing something is watchable: the cure machine fires, the coaster runs, the house upgrades with an animation.
lot_driven_mechanics: Two Point Hospital patient flow: every patient is a physical body that walks reception desk -> GP's Office -> diagnosis rooms -> back to GP -> treatment room. Queues form as literal lines of people outside room doors; an overloaded GP office is visible as a corridor full of bodies before any panel says so. Room adjacency is gameplay: clustering diagnosis rooms shortens the walking the player can literally watch.

Two Point Hospital room construction: rooms are dragged as floor blueprints (min sizes 2x3-4x5); required items appear as a checklist with yellow starburst icons; the door is mandatory to validate; 'footprint' markers around each placed item show whether staff/patients can reach it; the room only activates when the green checkmark is accepted. The build UI is painted onto the floor, not in a form.

Two Point Hospital illness-as-costume: diseases are worn on the body - Lightheadedness is a literal lightbulb head, Pandemic a pan on the head - and each maps to one themed treatment room whose cure machine performs a slapstick spectacle (the De-Lux-O-Luxe unscrews the bulb and screws on a 3D-printed head). The player learns the illness->room mapping by watching, not by reading.

Two Point Hospital maintenance/dirt: machines visibly smoke when degraded, vomit and litter accumulate on the floor, and janitors physically walk to fix them - hygiene and upkeep have no abstract meter that matters more than what the floor looks like.

Planet Zoo habitat editing: while the player paints terrain/water/plants inside a habitat, per-species requirement bars (terrain types, space, shelter, plant coverage) update live and turn red/orange/green in place - the validation UI runs during sculpting, so building the enclosure IS filling in the animal's needs sheet.

Planet Zoo / Planet Coaster 2 heatmaps: view modes repaint the actual park by guest mood/hunger/thirst, staff morale, utility (power/water) coverage, scenery impact, and finances; the Animal Welfare view whites out the world and tints each animal red (unhappy) to green (happy), so problems are found by looking at the lot, not a table.

Planet Coaster placement ghosts: facilities, staff buildings and (in PC2) power/water sources project their coverage radius on the ground during placement - range is negotiated spatially before commitment.

Parkitect physical logistics: goods enter through a Deliveries building at the park edge as crates; Haulers carry crates on foot to shops, or the player builds Depots fed by underground pneumatic tubes/conveyor belts; a shop with a broken or too-long route visibly runs out of stock. The supply chain is a road network you can watch operate (devlog 110: 'it should be fun and makes sense for gameplay reasons').

Parkitect backstage pressure: guests who see haulers, crates, depots or trash bags lose 'immersion'/'decoration' rating, which pushes players to build hidden staff-only paths and service corridors behind scenery - the lot naturally grows a front-of-house and a backstage, like a real park (or a 1948 studio).

Parkitect staff zones: haulers and janitors are assigned to spatial zones (e.g., a zone stretching from a depot to its shops) drawn on the map - labor allocation is a territory you paint, not a slider.

Frostpunk heat-as-geometry: the city is rings around one central Generator; heat is a radius, placing a Steam Hub previews its heat ring, and the temperature overlay tints ground and buildings by warmth. Cold homes produce visibly sick citizens who fill Medical Posts - the causal chain (radius -> cold home -> sick worker -> lost labor) is spatial end to end.

Anno 1800 status icons: broken chains announce themselves above the building - pause icon, insufficient-workforce icon, missing-input/zero-productivity icon, storage-full, no-street-connection. Residences grow a glowing upgrade arrow when their needs are fulfilled, so the next goal literally sprouts from the rooftops of your own town.
interaction_grammar: Click any person -> a card about THEM that points back into the world: a Two Point Hospital patient card shows health/happiness bars, their diagnosed illness, and an icon of the room they are currently queuing for, plus direct verbs ('Send Home', 'Send for Treatment'); Planet Coaster guests are individually named and inspectable for wellbeing and thoughts; Planet Zoo animals open the Animal Information Panel with welfare bars (nutrition, social, space, habitat, enrichment) and a jump-to-Zoopedia reference.

Click any building/room -> state plus the one relevant verb: TPH rooms show prestige, assigned staff and queue and offer edit/copy; Parkitect shops show stock level and price; Anno factories show productivity percentage, input/output buffers and a pause toggle. The panel never contains the whole management layer - just this object's slice.

Build = drag a blueprint in the world, then satisfy a visible checklist: TPH's required-items list with starburst icons and the green checkmark to commission the room is the canonical form; Planet Zoo does the same with live red/green requirement bars during habitat editing; nothing becomes operational while a requirement is unmet, and the unmet item is named.

Verbs are discovered at the moment of need, not in a manual: TPH surfaces 'hire a doctor' only when a built GP office sits unstaffed (the room card shows an empty staff slot); Anno surfaces the next production chain by graying out what the newly unlocked population tier demands; Parkitect teaches depots when the player watches a hauler trek across the whole park.

Menus mirror the world's categories, not the simulation's internals: TPH's build menu is Rooms/Items/Staff; Anno's construction menu is organized by population tier so the menu itself is a tech tree of chains. Where menus stop mirroring the world (Planet Coaster's menus-within-menus) players get lost - reviewers single this out.

Time control is a first-class verb: pause/fast-forward lets players stop the world to read it (TPH, Frostpunk, Anno all support it); Frostpunk pairs every crisis event with pause so reading never costs the player the city.
attention_language: Persistent objective checklist instead of modal tutorial: Two Point Hospital's star objectives (e.g., 'Cure 15 patients', 'Reach hospital level 5') sit in an always-visible panel and tick off live; the first career levels simply gate which objectives exist, so the checklist IS the tutorial.

Thought/help bubbles anchored to bodies: TPH patients and staff emit bubbles (unhappiness, confusion, 'needs guidance' bubbles over a swamped GP office); Planet Coaster guests think inspectable thoughts; the bubble marks WHERE the problem is standing.

Comedy PA announcer as ambient telemetry: TPH's tannoy voice ('Patients are reminded not to die in the corridors') converts aggregate state (deaths, queues, litter) into flavored audio warnings that never require a click.

Click-to-zoom notifications: Planet Zoo alert toasts jump the camera to the affected animal on click; Frostpunk side notifications pan to the site of the event (a fight, a body); Anno 1800's right-edge ticker jumps to the fire/quest/ship. The notification is a teleport, not a paragraph.

Status icons floating over buildings (Anno): missing workforce, missing input, storage full, paused, no street connection - each stall names its cause at the building; the residence upgrade arrow is the inverse: an icon that says 'next step available here'.

Color painted on the world: Planet Zoo's welfare view (white world, red-to-green animals), heatmaps for mood/coverage/scenery, TPH room prestige tinting, Frostpunk's temperature overlay. Color modes are opt-in lenses over the same lot - though Planet Zoo shows the failure mode: auto-popping a bright white heatmap when placing certain objects annoyed players enough to demand a toggle.
Radius previews during placement (Planet Coaster facilities, Frostpunk steam hubs, Anno pubs/markets): the game answers 'will this reach?' before the player commits.

Escalating physical symptoms as alarm: TPH queues spill into corridors and patients die visibly; Parkitect trash piles and 'out of stock' shops; Frostpunk graves. The alarm state is diegetic - the lot looks wrong before any number does.

Advisor characters used sparingly or it backfires: Planet Zoo's voiced career characters (Bernie Goodwin, Nancy Jones) narrate objectives, and community verdict is that 'they never shut up,' with more puns than actual hints - proof that voice-over cannot substitute for world legibility.
first_session_experience: The gold standard is Two Point Hospital's Hogsport: one small plot, a non-optional but fully diegetic first level. The objectives panel says 'Build a Reception'; patients immediately stream through the doors and mill in the lobby, creating visible pressure with nowhere to go. Next objective: build a GP's Office - the blueprint drag teaches minimum size, the yellow-starburst required-items list teaches furnishing, the green checkmark commissions it. The room then sits idle with an empty staff slot, which motivates 'hire a Doctor' (candidate cards teach qualifications). Only one or two illnesses exist on this level (e.g., Lightheadedness - literal lightbulb heads walking your corridor), so when the GP diagnoses them the game demands exactly one treatment room, and the player watches the De-Lux machine cure someone - chain complete in ~20 minutes: reception -> GP -> diagnosis -> treatment, learned by following bodies, with each new system introduced by a person visibly stuck at the missing step. Anno 1800 does the tiered version: your first houses show unmet-need icons, clicking a need names the good, building the chain makes the upgrade arrow sprout. The anti-patterns from the same cohort: Planet Zoo's career opens with a narrated, hand-holding zoo players called 'the most boring gameplay experience' (watching, not doing); Parkitect's tutorial 'shows you little before pushing you in,' leaving depots and staff zones to be discovered via wiki; Planet Coaster's tutorials 'do a poor job' and its nested menus hide the management layer entirely.
criticisms_and_failures: Two Point Hospital queue/AI illegibility: players report many patients queuing for one diagnostic room while identical rooms sit empty, and all staff taking breaks simultaneously while queues explode - when the sim's dispatcher is opaque, a legible world makes the wrongness MORE maddening because you can see it and not fix it (Steam threads: 'The diagnostic/queue system still feels broken').

Two Point Hospital positive-feedback flood: rising reputation pulls patients in faster than rooms can be built, tipping late-game into micromanagement grind; reviewers also call the late game repetitive and a time sink (waiting for hireable staff to rotate into the limited candidate pool).

Planet Coaster (1 and 2): 'menus hidden in menus all the way down'; newcomers can't locate key tools; management judged shallow under the beautiful building layer; guest pathfinding produces false explanations ('couldn't find a way to ride' while standing next to the entrance) - a world that explains itself wrongly is worse than silence.

Planet Zoo: heatmap auto-popup whiteout when placing education/power objects irritated players (threads asking to 'turn off heat map pop up'); notification volume and welfare micromanagement across a big zoo overwhelm; career narrators talk constantly with more puns than hints; the tutorial plays itself ('like watching a video on YouTube').

Planet Zoo depth wall: the per-animal simulation is praised, but the sheer number of bars (nutrition/social/space/habitat/enrichment x every animal) means mid-game players live in alert triage rather than on the lot - inspection depth without aggregation becomes homework.

Parkitect: steep learning curve, minimal tutorial; core physical-logistics systems (depots, tubes, staff zones) are the best ideas in the game and are the least taught - community guides fill the gap.

Frostpunk: the world layer is superb but the abstract layers cost clicks - the Book of Laws requires zooming/clicking to read each law, mode swaps are slow, 'pointless animations wasting time'; some players flatly call the UI bad despite the acclaimed art direction.

Anno 1800: floating building icons explain single buildings but never aggregate - Ubisoft had to patch in a Statistics/production spreadsheet screen because players couldn't answer 'am I net-positive on beer?' from the world alone. World-level legibility needs a ledger backstop.
lessons_for_project_studio: Run 'Hogsport for Hollywood': the first session should be one objective checklist, permanently on screen, whose steps are the filmmaking chain itself - 'Commission a screenplay' -> 'Read the draft' -> 'Audition a lead' -> 'Assemble the package' -> 'Greenlight' -> 'Watch Week 1 of shooting'. Each objective unlocks only when the previous one's physical consequence appears on the lot. No modal tutorial, no narrator; the checklist plus the lot carries it.

Make the movie a physical artifact that travels: like Parkitect's crates, the screenplay should be a visible bound script - a writer types at Development & Casting (paper piling up = progress), a courier walks the finished draft to the player's desk at Administration, the approved script physically moves to the soundstage when greenlit. A player who watches the script move has learned the pipeline without opening a panel.

Steal TPH's required-items grammar for the greenlight package: the package is a 'room blueprint' with slots (script, director, lead, supporting, budget) shown as a checklist with starburst icons on the missing slots; the Greenlight button is the green checkmark and stays disabled with the missing slot named. The player should never wonder why they can't greenlight.

Put Anno status icons over every building: Soundstage shows 'no production assigned' / 'awaiting cast' / 'rehearsing (3 wks)' / 'stalled: no director'; Development shows a quill-and-page icon with draft progress; the Gate shows premiere/press icons. Every weekly-tick stall must name its cause above the building where it stalled.

Anno's upgrade arrow, translated: when a package becomes greenlightable, the Development & Casting building sprouts a glowing marker (a klieg light beam is period-perfect). The building announces the available verb; the player walks the camera into the next step rather than hunting menus.

Every notification is a teleport (Planet Zoo/Frostpunk/Anno rule): 'Your screenplay draft is ready' zooms to the writer handing it over; 'Audition scheduled' zooms to actors lining up outside Development & Casting; 'Production stalled' zooms to the empty soundstage. Never a toast that only opens a panel.

Make people wear their state like TPH illnesses wear costumes: an idle contracted actor lounges by the gate; an unhappy director paces; a star in rehearsal carries sides (script pages); crew push flats and cameras between Scenery/Service and the stage during preproduction. Click any person -> card showing their current phase, destination building, and mood, with the destination as an icon (TPH's queue-room icon).

Make shooting a watchable spectacle (the cure-machine lesson): lights, camera dolly, director's chair, slate-clap per scene on the soundstage - spectacle is how TPH teaches which room does what, and it doubles as the reward for a correct greenlight. Consider dailies screenings and a premiere at the Gate as the visible 'patient cured' moment.

Adopt Parkitect's front/backstage split: the 1948 lot has glamour faces (Gate, stars' entrances, premiere crowds, studio tours) and service circulation (Scenery/Service flats, catering, extras). If tour guests or press see backstage chaos, publicity suffers - this makes lot layout a real decision, exactly as immersion does in Parkitect.

Use overlays as opt-in lenses, never auto-popping: one or two view modes maximum (e.g., 'Buzz' tinting productions by publicity heat, 'Morale' tinting people red-green like Planet Zoo's welfare view). Planet Zoo's whiteout complaints show forced overlays break trust in the world view.

Keep the dispatcher legible or pay double (TPH's queue lesson): with a deterministic weekly tick you have an advantage - when a person stands idle, clicking them must state the exact blocking condition ('waiting: Stage 2 occupied until week 14'). TPH's worst reviews come from visible wrongness with invisible cause.

Add the ledger backstop early (Anno's patched-in statistics lesson): world legibility answers 'what is stuck HERE'; a single studio ledger (slate of productions, phase, weeks remaining, cash burn) answers 'how is the studio doing'. One screen, reachable from Administration - do not make players derive aggregates by panning the lot.

Do not ship a chatty advisor: Planet Zoo proves voiced hand-holding gets muted and resented. If 1948 flavor wants a voice, use TPH's model - a lot loudspeaker/switchboard operator delivering short diegetic status gags ('Stage 3 is dark again, Mr. Mayer') as ambient telemetry, never as instruction.

game: RollerCoaster Tycoon 1/2 (Chris Sawyer, 1999/2002) and RollerCoaster Tycoon 3 (Frontier, 2004)
core_loop: Moment-to-moment: build or place a ride/path/shop on the terrain, watch guests physically walk to it and queue, read their thoughts and the news ticker for problems, and adjust price, staffing, or layout. Session-level: grow cash into bigger custom coasters — build track piece by piece, TEST it with an empty train while stats populate, open it, watch the queue fill and income tick up, then defend the investment against breakdowns, litter, and crashes. The scenario objective (e.g. "250 guests and park rating 600 by October, Year 1") gives each session a finish line, and completing it unlocks the next, harder park. The player never leaves the park view; every management fact has a physical address.
lot_driven_mechanics: Rides are persistent named objects living on the map: every placed ride is auto-named ('Wooden Roller Coaster 1', renameable), stays for the whole scenario, and accrues history — age, declining reliability, lifetime customers, running cost, profit. Clicking its sprite on the lot opens ITS window; the Rides list menu is just an index back into the world.

Coaster construction is done in the world, not a form: track laid piece-by-piece on real terrain with a ghost preview, cost deducted per piece, chain lifts and supports drawn as you go. Terrain and existing buildings ARE the design constraints.

Test mode is a physical rehearsal: the ride window's View tab has a closed/testing/open traffic-light control; 'Test' sends an empty train around the circuit on the lot while the Measurements tab fills with excitement/intensity/nausea ratings, max speed, ride time, G-forces, and the Graphs tab plots velocity/altitude/Gs (per the [RCT wiki](https://rct.fandom.com/wiki/Hints_and_Tips) and [game manual](http://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steam/apps/285310/manuals/rollercoaster_tycoon.pdf)). An incomplete or over-fast circuit crashes visibly during test — failure is shown on the ground before real money and lives are staked.
Queues are physical demand meters: the queue path is built tile by tile, guests literally stand in it, and its length is instant feedback on popularity vs. throughput vs. price.

Guests are visible individuals: each peep is named ('Guest 112', renameable), carries visible balloons/maps/umbrellas, vomits when nauseated, sits on benches, and can be picked up with the tweezers tool and dropped elsewhere. Clicking any peep opens their window with needs, cash, and current [thoughts](https://mechanicsingames.wordpress.com/2019/07/12/guest-thoughts-roller-coaster-tycoon/).

Park hygiene is drawn on the lot: litter, vomit pools, vandalized benches, and unmowed grass are rendered on tiles; handymen visibly sweep, mow, empty bins, and water gardens. Upkeep is watched, not read off a meter.

Breakdown theater: a broken ride visibly stalls with the train stuck, the ticker announces it, the ride window names the fault, and a mechanic physically WALKS to the ride exit and performs an animated repair — station brakes are fixed by hammering them five times (per the [Breakdown wiki](https://rct.fandom.com/wiki/Breakdown)). If paths don't reach the exit, the mechanic never arrives and the ride stays broken — the dependency is spatial.

Crashes are consequence-as-spectacle: a Station Brakes Failure sends a train through the station — explosion on the lot, guests die, park rating nose-dives, guest count drops ([Crash wiki](https://rct.fandom.com/wiki/Crash)). Disaster happens where you can see it, at the thing you built.
Staff management is painting the ground: patrol areas are drawn as zones directly on paths; staff are placed by dropping their sprite on a tile.

The park entrance is a physical economic choke point: guests spawn at the map edge, walk the road in, and pay at the gate; advertising campaigns and awards manifest as visibly denser crowds streaming through it.
Scenery is mechanically real: placing trees and themed scenery near track raises a coaster's excitement rating — decorating the lot is a stat action, not cosmetics.

RCT3 adds inhabiting your product: CoasterCam rides your own coaster POV, peep-cam follows any guest first-person, VIP guests walk a route you must impress, peeps arrive in families, and MixMaster firework shows are staged over the park at night ([RCT3 wiki](https://rct.fandom.com/wiki/RollerCoaster_Tycoon_3), [MobyGames](https://www.mobygames.com/game/15734/rollercoaster-tycoon-3/)).
interaction_grammar: Universal rule: click any object in the world (ride, guest, staff member, park gate) and its persistent, movable, non-modal window opens. Many windows can be open at once; a window is the object's dossier and follows it live.

The ride window is one object with ~9 icon-tab lenses: View (live thumbnail + open/test/close traffic light), Vehicles (train config), Operating options (mode, dispatch timing), Color scheme, Music, Measurements (excitement/intensity/nausea + test stats), Graphs (velocity/altitude/G plots), Income & costs (set ticket price, see profit/hr, running cost), Customers (recent riders, popularity, satisfaction) — documented in the [manual](http://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steam/apps/285310/manuals/rollercoaster_tycoon.pdf) and [RCT wiki](https://rct.fandom.com/wiki/Ride_Operation_Options).

Build verbs live on one small fixed top toolbar (new ride, path, scenery, terrain, staff, finances, rides list, guests list); every OTHER verb is discovered by clicking the world. Menus are indexes into the lot, never a parallel reality: clicking a ride's row in the Rides list opens the same window as clicking its sprite.

Direct-manipulation verbs: tweezers pick up and relocate guests/staff; patrol zones are painted; renaming is a text field on the object's window; the price is a spinner on the ride's own Income tab, not a global pricing screen.
Clicking a news-ticker message jumps the camera to its subject — message and place are one thing.
Everything is hover-labeled; the grammar never changes across 20+ ride types, so learning one ride window teaches all of them.
RCT3 keeps the same object-window grammar but adds a free 3D camera and in-world cameras (CoasterCam, peep cam); the trade was glanceability for immersion.
attention_language: News ticker as the attention spine: messages slide in at the bottom of the screen with a per-type icon and sound — 'Wooden Roller Coaster 1 has broken down', 'Guest 112 is lost and can't find the park exit', 'New ride now available: ...', 'Your park has received an award!', crash announcements. Clicking one jumps the camera to the subject; a Recent Messages toolbar button keeps the archive ([OpenRCT2 docs/issues](https://github.com/OpenRCT2/OpenRCT2/issues/1423) preserve this design).

Guest thoughts as distributed telemetry: 'I'm not paying that much!' (price > perceived value), 'It was great value!' (underpriced), 'I want to go home', 'I feel sick', 'The paths are disgusting' — feedback attached to individual people, aggregated per-ride in the Customers tab. The game guides via implicit crowd voice instead of tooltips ([Mechanics in Games analysis](https://mechanicsingames.wordpress.com/2019/07/12/guest-thoughts-roller-coaster-tycoon/)).

Color/state codes: the open/test/closed traffic light (green/yellow/red flags at the ride entrance and in the window); ride list rows show status; guest happiness rendered as face icons, angry guests turn visibly red.

Animation as alarm: a stalled train = broken ride; an empty queue = pricing/path problem; a vomit trail = intensity problem; the mechanic sprite walking toward the ride = help is en route; denser gate crowds = marketing working.
An always-visible status strip: cash, guest count, park rating, and date sit at the screen bottom — the three scenario-relevant numbers are never more than a glance away.
Sound as event grammar: award fanfare, crash explosion and screams, ride-specific music, crowd murmur that swells with density.
Scenario verdict messages: the objective deadline resolves in-fiction ('You have completed the objective / failed') rather than a menu screen.
first_session_experience: RCT1's Forest Frontiers is the canonical cold start. The objective is one sentence stated before you load in: 250 guests and a 600 park rating by October, Year 1 ([Forest Frontiers wiki](https://rct.fandom.com/wiki/Forest_Frontiers)). You begin with cash, a gate, one stub of path, and an empty flat meadow — the emptiness itself says 'build here'. The toolbar offers few verbs; the obvious one (New Ride) opens a short list of pre-designed gentle rides, sidestepping custom coaster construction entirely for the first hour. Placing a ride walks you through the full chain by construction order: footprint, entrance, exit, then the game won't produce customers until you drag a queue and connect it to the path — the empty queue and idle ride ARE the error message. Open the ride with the traffic light, and guests visibly stream from the map edge through your gate into the line; cash ticks up per rider on the ride's own Income tab. Problems announce themselves through the ticker and through clicking any guest to read thoughts. RCT1 also shipped a watch-it-play tutorial: chosen from the main menu, the game builds a gentle ride and a roller coaster in Forest Frontiers by itself while you watch the cursor work — teaching by demonstration on the real lot ([StrategyWiki](https://strategywiki.org/wiki/RollerCoaster_Tycoon/Forest_Frontiers)). The scenario sequence then acts as the real tutorial: each early park isolates one new system (per [Shamus Young's retrospective](https://www.shamusyoung.com/twentysidedtale/?p=57871): basic building, then inherited infrastructure, then pathfinding terrain, then coaster maintenance, then scale), and research drip-feeds new ride types one ticker message at a time so the build menu never overwhelms.
criticisms_and_failures: Silent spatial dependencies: if no path reaches a ride's exit, mechanics can never repair it; the game spams 'is still broken down' without ever stating the cause — players got stuck for hours, and [OpenRCT2 issue #19767](https://github.com/OpenRCT2/OpenRCT2/issues/19767) exists precisely because the original never messaged the real problem.

Staff micromanagement failure: handymen mow distant lawns while vomit piles up on the midway unless the player hand-paints patrol areas — the game never teaches that patrol zones are the fix ([Mechanic wiki](https://rct.fandom.com/wiki/Mechanic), Steam forum threads on 'mechanics not fixing rides').

Dumb guest pathfinding punished layout experimentation: complex or looping paths bred hundreds of lost, angry guests ('I'm lost!'), tanking the rating; the counter-tool (no-entry banners) is obscure and untaught.

Price/value feedback lives only in individual thoughts, so new players systematically mispriced rides for hours before noticing 'I'm not paying that much' — the aggregate signal (per-ride thought summaries) is buried in a tab.

Tiny unlabeled icon tabs on 640x480-era windows: the ride window's nine tabs are learned by hover-and-poke; reviewers noted RCT2 shipped 'no improvement in graphics, sound, interface, or gameplay' and a camera that 'cannot be moved in 3D' ([Metacritic critic reviews](https://www.metacritic.com/game/rollercoaster-tycoon-2/critic-reviews/?platform=pc)).

RCT2 abandoned RCT1's teaching staircase: all scenario groups open at once plus 'fairly ordinary objectives' meant nothing sequenced learning for newcomers — critics called it 'more of the same' and it leaned entirely on players already trained by RCT1.

Unfair invisible catastrophe: RCT1's Station Brakes Failure crash is nearly unpreventable on some designs and the mitigation (one-train operation, sub-20mph station entry) is community lore, not in-game knowledge ([Crash wiki](https://rct.fandom.com/wiki/Crash)).

RCT3 traded readability for fidelity: choppy camera, 'nearly impossible' 3D path building, performance collapse in large parks, and freezes when placing big pre-built coasters ([GameFAQs](https://gamefaqs.gamespot.com/pc/919973-rollercoaster-tycoon-3/reviews/82916), [GamingTrend](https://gamingtrend.com/reviews/rollercoaster-tycoon-3-complete-edition-review-get-me-off-of-this-coaster/)) — the isometric sprites' at-a-glance park state was lost to 3D clutter.
RCT3's added peep depth (families, VIP routes, peep editor) added simulation noise more than management meaning; reviewers praised the CoasterCam spectacle but panned the moment-to-moment interface.
lessons_for_project_studio: Make each production a persistent named object with ONE window and tabbed lenses, exactly like the ride window: View (live camera on wherever the production physically is now), Package (script/director/cast = RCT's Vehicles/Operating tabs), Dailies (test stats), Income, Audience (aggregated reactions). Auto-name it ('Untitled Western No. 1'), let renaming be one click, and let it accrue lifetime history (grosses, awards) the way a coaster accrues lifetime customers.

The chain must be walkable, and each link must be a place: commissioning puts a writer visibly at a desk in Development & Casting; the finished script is physically carried to the player's desk; auditioning actors queue outside the stage like an RCT queue path; greenlighting moves the company onto a soundstage. RCT proves players learn a hidden system by watching bodies move through buildings — the movement IS the tutorial.

Give every production an RCT traffic light: a develop / rehearse / shoot control on the production itself. Rehearsal is your Test mode — run it and watch predicted stats (script quality, chemistry, projected audience score — your excitement/intensity/nausea triple) populate a Measurements tab, with problems surfacing visibly (a star storming off the rehearsal stage = the test-run crash) BEFORE the shooting budget is committed.

Build the news ticker as the attention spine now: every event is a message with an icon, a sound, and an address — 'Shooting has halted on Stage 2', 'Script for Untitled Western No. 1 has been delivered', 'Variety: your picture won Best Drama' — clicking jumps the camera there, with a Recent Messages archive. In RCT this single widget carries the entire game's urgency.

Replace dashboards with distributed thoughts: writers, actors, and crew on the lot emit thought bubbles ('This script needs another draft', 'I won't work for scale'), and preview-audience guests at a screening emit the value/price feedback RCT guests give ('I'm not paying that much!' → your ticket/quality signal), aggregated on the production's Audience tab. Feedback attached to visible people teaches without tutorials and preserves 1948 fiction.

Sequence learning with scenario objectives, not tutorial text: first studio = one soundstage, generous cash, objective 'Release one picture with audience score 60 by end of 1949'; later scenarios each isolate one new system (a studio with an inherited troubled production; a genre-locked studio; a bank-debt studio), mirroring how Forest Frontiers → Dynamite Dunes → Leafy Lake each added exactly one complication. Consider RCT3's Apprentice/Entrepreneur/Tycoon tiered goals so one lot teaches three depths ([Career mode wiki](https://rct.fandom.com/wiki/Career_mode)).

Ship RCT1's watch-it-play tutorial: a scripted demo where the studio (an 'assistant' cursor) walks one B-picture through commission → audition → greenlight → shoot → premiere on the real lot while the player watches. This is the cheapest possible answer to 'a new player cannot figure out how to make their first movie'.

Fix RCT's documented failure, don't copy it: when a phase is blocked, always message the cause with the blocking dependency named and clickable ('Rehearsal cannot start: no director attached'), and show the idle person standing at the blocked building. RCT's silent 'still broken down' loop is its single most complained-about UX hole.

Consequence must be spectacle at a place: a flop is an empty premiere forecourt, a scandal is a press mob at the Gate, an overrun is visibly idle crew on a lit soundstage — RCT's crash-and-explosion proves a visible disaster at the thing you built teaches cost faster than any red number.

Use physical queues as your demand meters: the audition line's length shows casting draw; the crowd density at the Gate on opening week IS the box-office chart. RCT's queue path is the best-ever diegetic KPI — steal it.

Show labor to make the simulation trusted: typewriters going in Development, carpenters building flats, film cans carried to post — RCT's sweeping handymen and hammer-swinging mechanics are why players believe the sim. But skip patrol-area micromanagement; assignment should be automatic with visible results.

Defend isometric readability as a feature: RCT3's decline into camera fights and 3D clutter shows that the 2D lot with high-contrast state animation (idle vs. working, lit vs. dark stage) is itself the primary UI — spend art budget on legible states, not fidelity.

game: Zoo Tycoon (Blue Fang Games, 2001) and Zoo Tycoon 2 (Blue Fang Games, 2004)
core_loop: Moment-to-moment: draw a fence loop to create an exhibit, adopt an animal into it, read the animal's need bars and the zookeeper's plain-language recommendations, then physically edit the enclosure (paint terrain/biome, place foliage, rocks, shelters, toys) while watching the suitability meter climb into the green. Session-level: happy animals attract and please guests, guests spend and donate, money and zoo rating (fame stars in ZT2) unlock more species and buildings, which demand bigger and harder exhibits; neglect produces visible decay (filth, sick animals, fence damage, escapes) that pulls the player back into the world to fix it. The entire management layer is expressed as things standing on the map: the player rarely acts through abstract dashboards, they act by placing, painting, and clicking objects in the zoo itself.
lot_driven_mechanics: Exhibit creation by enclosure: drawing a complete loop of fence pieces on the map automatically instantiates a named game object ('Exhibit 1'), which the sim then reasons about (suitability, contained animals, cleanliness). The world geometry IS the data model - there is no separate 'create exhibit' form.

Suitability tuning by physical editing: the exhibit's suitability rating (0-100) is a function of terrain tiles, elevation, foliage, rocks, toys, shelters, fence type, and co-housed species. Improving it means painting terrain (ZT1 tile swaps; ZT2's biome brush that paints savannah/tundra/rainforest ground directly) and placing objects - and the animal's suitability/biome need meter moves in real time as you edit, so cause and effect are learned kinesthetically.

Animals wear their state in the world: content animals show green smiley faces, stressed animals show red frowny faces above/on them (ZT1); in ZT2 sick animals visibly droop and dirty animals attract attention. You can diagnose a failing exhibit from camera range before opening any panel.

Physical delivery of management decisions (ZT2): adopted animals arrive as crates placed on the map; the 'New Animal Arrivals' campaign scenario literally hands the player three crates and asks them to place each into the exhibit whose biome matches - selecting the crate opens an info panel saying what animal is inside. The management verb (adopt) produces a watchable physical event (crate opens, animal walks out).

Filth as rendered objects: animal poop piles and path litter are individual visible objects in the world; dirty exhibits upset animals and guests, and zookeepers physically pathfind to each poop pile to rake it. Cleanliness is not a hidden stat - you can see the mess accumulating from the air.

Staff as visible laborers: zookeepers assigned to exhibits walk to food dishes, fill them, wash animals, heal the sick, rake poop; maintenance workers sweep paths and repair fences; you verify care is happening by watching it happen (or not happening - a keeper stuck outside a gate is a visible bug/failure).

Escapes as physical crises: fences have a strength value that deteriorates visibly with wear; when an animal's strength exceeds the fence's remaining strength it bashes through, wanders the paths, and guests scream and scatter (and can be attacked). Resolution is also physical: repair/rebuild the fence, re-contain the animal. The alert ('Snow Leopard 1 has escaped into Exhibit 1') names world objects.

Guest economy expressed spatially: guests physically walk paths, cluster at exhibit fences to view animals, drop money in donation boxes the player places next to exhibits, and queue at food stands and bathrooms. Amenity problems are placement problems - a bathroom too far from a popular exhibit produces complaining guests at that location.

ZT2's first-person Zoo Guest/Zookeeper mode: the player can drop down into the zoo, walk it at eye level, and do the chores themselves - rake poop, fill troughs and water dishes, brush and heal animals, take photos - making the zoo an inhabitable place, not a spreadsheet with a skin.
interaction_grammar: Universal click-to-inspect: clicking ANY entity - animal, guest, staff member, building, exhibit fence, crate - opens a same-shaped info panel (portrait, name, need meters). Because every panel rhymes, learning one teaches all of them.

The advisor verb: on an animal's panel, clicking the zookeeper icon opens the 'zookeeper recommendations' panel, which translates hidden requirements into a plain-language shopping list ('unhappy with the foliage', 'prefers savannah terrain', 'needs a place to hide'). In ZT2, clicking an animal and then a zookeeper 'displays exactly what needs purchasing' (GameRevolution). This is pull-based expert help: the player asks, the world answers in buy-menu vocabulary.

Diagnosis and remedy share one vocabulary: the recommendation says 'more foliage' and the build menu has a foliage tab full of placeable trees; the fix is always a physical object you place, never an abstract toggle. This closed loop (read complaint -> buy named thing -> place it -> watch meter rise) is the game's entire pedagogy.

Build menus are palettes of world objects: fences, terrain types, foliage, rocks, shelters, toys, food stands, bathrooms, donation boxes. Every purchase resolves into placement on the map; there are no stat-only upgrades.

Terrain/biome brush as a verb: select a terrain type and paint the ground inside an exhibit; in ZT2 the brush sculpts hills and ponds too. The reviewer consensus was that this was 'surprisingly simple to use'.

Direct manipulation hand: the player can pick up and relocate animals and objects, and in ZT1 even pick up guests (famously including dropping complainers into the lion exhibit) - the cursor is a hand in the world, not a menu pointer.

Guests as sensors: clicking any guest shows their stats and current thoughts ('This zoo is something else!', 'The playground is wonderful fun!'), turning any individual walking past into a free consultant on what to build next.

Reference layer one click deep (ZT2): the Zoopedia is an in-game encyclopedia entry for every animal, object, plant, fence and path - dietary habits, preferred biome, species compatibilities - readable BEFORE purchase, from the same UI.

Messages reference named world objects: Message Box entries like 'Orca 1 can't find any food' or 'Snow Leopard 1 has escaped into Exhibit 1' use the same names as the panels, so text alerts, panels, and the map are one namespace.
attention_language: Emoticon overlays: green smiley face = content animal, red frowny face = stressed animal, shown on the animal itself and its panel (ZT1). The cheapest possible glyph, readable at full zoom-out.

Color-coded need meters: ZT1 shows horizontal bars 0-100 (green fulfilled / yellow partial / red unmet); ZT2 shows square need icons with a vertical fill going green ('satisfied') -> yellow ('pressing') -> red ('critical'). When a need goes red, a red notification message fires.

The Message Box / on-screen message stream: concrete, named, actionable alerts at the top of the screen - 'Orca 1 is not happy', 'Orca 1 can't find any food', 'Lion 2 is sick', 'Snow Leopard 1 has escaped into Exhibit 1', 'Your zoo is running on low money'. Subject + place + problem in one line.

Aggregated guest sentiment broadcasts: 'Guests are complaining that your zoo is too dirty', 'Guests would like to see a greater variety of animals in your zoo' - the crowd speaks as a chorus when a pattern emerges, so the player doesn't have to poll individuals.

Ambient physical warnings: accumulating poop piles and litter, visibly deteriorating fence sections, sick animals lying down, guests running and screaming from an escaped animal - the zoo degrades on camera as an analog alarm that precedes or accompanies text alerts.

Pull-based advisor rather than push-only nagging: the zookeeper recommendations panel waits to be asked, which keeps the alert channel for genuine events and makes the player feel like the diagnostician.

Macro progress meters: zoo rating / guest happiness ratings in ZT1 and the zoo fame star level in ZT2 (rising fame unlocks new animals and objects) give a single always-visible 'how am I doing' gauge whose growth is itself the reward schedule.
first_session_experience: A new ZT1 player in freeform mode starts with modest cash and a deliberately tiny, cheap adoption list (low-maintenance starter animals), so the first decision space is small. They draw a fence loop - the game instantly recognizes 'Exhibit 1' - and drop in an animal. Within seconds the animal shows a red frowny face: failure is immediate, visible, located on a body, and non-catastrophic. Clicking the animal opens a panel with a few filled bars (the fourth is exhibit suitability); clicking the zookeeper icon on that panel yields an explicit recipe in plain English: prefers savannah terrain, wants more foliage, needs a shelter. Every noun in that list corresponds to a tab in the build menu. The player paints savannah tiles and places trees and rocks WHILE the suitability bar visibly climbs, converting a hidden formula into a hand-eye loop; when the bar turns green the frown becomes a smile and guests gather at the fence and start dropping donations. Hire a zookeeper, place a bathroom and food stand when guest complaints appear, done - the whole viable-exhibit chain is learned in 15-30 minutes with no manual because (a) the first failure is instant and legible, (b) the advisor converts requirements into shopping-list vocabulary, (c) the remedy is physical placement with real-time meter feedback, and (d) the reward (crowds and donations) is acted out on the map. ZT2 adds an explicit 3-part tutorial (camera controls; basic gameplay - place iron-bar fence, adopt a Bengal tiger, use the biome brush, hire staff, place guest buildings; advanced topics) and then a first campaign scenario, 'New Animal Arrivals', that is pure worked-example pedagogy: three crated animals, three prepared biome areas, match crate to biome, with the crate's info panel telling you what's inside.
criticisms_and_failures: Opaque derived metrics broke trust: the Legacy of Games retrospective describes a perfect exhibit - ideal for the animals, loved by every guest - that still showed '0 stars for popularity' and generated no money, with 'no clue' and 'no hints' on how to fix it. When one number in an otherwise legible game refuses to decompose, players hit a wall.

Depth criticism: PC Gamer scored ZT1 48/100 for simplistic mechanics; IGN (6.9) said 'there really isn't much exciting to keep you occupied here after playing for a while.' Visible feedback taught the game brilliantly but the loop plateaued once the recipe was mastered.

ZT2 message spam: GameSpot's review noted that with unhappy guests and animals 'you'll be overwhelmed by messages and things to do,' because ZT2 shifted work from autonomous ZT1-style zookeepers onto the player. An attention system that fires per-entity does not scale with zoo size.

Advisor/metric contradictions: the community documented cases (e.g., the camel) where the zookeeper recommendations panel reported unhappiness with foliage even when the numeric suitability rating looked high - when the advisor and the meters disagree, the player no longer knows which channel to believe.

Sim legibility depends on believable behavior: GameRevolution slammed ZT2 for guests inexplicably walking past empty trash cans to use distant full ones, animals getting stuck and 'moonwalking' against objects, plus 'unintuitive controls and confusing menu structure.' A world-as-interface game is uniquely damaged when the world visibly behaves stupidly.

Suitability was guesswork without the advisor: nothing in the ZT1 world itself communicated a species' terrain percentages; the knowledge lived only in the recommendations panel and out-of-game guides (guides listing exact terrain recipes flourished for a reason). ZT2 moved this into the Zoopedia, but that split canonical knowledge across panels.
ZT1's limited zoom levels were called out by GameSpot - players managing through the world need to see the world at multiple scales.

Emergent physical events sometimes undermined tone and fairness: the notorious ZT1 emperor penguin glitch let penguins kill any other species, and escape violence (animals killing guests) sat oddly in a family game - physical crisis systems need tight edge-case control.
lessons_for_project_studio: Make the production the 'exhibit': a greenlit picture must be a named, selectable, followable world object anchored to a place - a card on the soundstage door reading 'Stage 2 - DESERT SERENADE - SHOOTING, week 3 of 6' - and every alert must reference it by name and place exactly like 'Snow Leopard 1 has escaped into Exhibit 1'. Clicking the stage opens the production's panel; the panel and the stage are the same object.

Adopt the frowny-face layer: put mood/status glyphs on people standing on the lot (a red glyph over the star sulking outside her dressing room, a script icon over the writer pacing at Development, a green glyph over a rehearsing cast). ZT proves problems should be visible at camera range before any panel opens - Project Studio's hidden-chain problem is precisely the absence of this layer.

One universal click-grammar: click ANY person, building, or production and get a same-shaped card (portrait, name, 3-5 meters, one advice button). ZT teaches itself because animal/guest/staff panels rhyme; actor/writer/director/picture/building cards must rhyme identically.

Steal the zookeeper-recommendations verb - this is the single highest-value transfer. Every production (and the studio itself) gets a pull-based advisor button (a Unit Production Manager or studio fixer) that converts state into a shopping list in the exact vocabulary of the player's verbs: 'DESERT SERENADE needs: a leading man (run Auditions at Casting), an approved budget (Administration), a director attached (Development).' The new player's question 'how do I make a movie?' is answered by clicking the fixer on their empty lot: 'You have no screenplay. Commission one at Development & Casting.'

Diagnosis and remedy must share one vocabulary and one click-path: if the fixer says 'no screenplay', the Development & Casting building's card must show a big 'Commission Screenplay' button using those same words. ZT's loop works because 'needs more foliage' maps 1:1 onto a foliage tab; any gap between advice-language and verb-language recreates the hidden chain.

Live meter while assembling: ZT1 players learned exhibit recipes by watching the suitability bar climb as they painted terrain. Show a package-strength/viability meter that visibly moves in real time as the player attaches script, director, cast, and budget to a package - greenlight readiness becomes something you tune by watching the needle, not a rule you must already know.

Physically deliver management decisions (ZT2's crates): commissioning a screenplay spawns a courier who walks a script package to Development; scheduling auditions spawns a visible line of actors outside Casting; greenlighting sends the cast walking to the soundstage. Each management click producing a watchable lot event is how the chain becomes learnable by observation - and the weekly tick can animate these as the week's happenings.

Filth-equivalent ambient degradation: represent drifting problems as physical scenes, not hidden numbers - idle contract players playing cards outside an unused stage (payroll burning), a dark cobwebbed soundstage (capacity wasted), press milling at the Gate (publicity opportunity), empty seats at Administration (no release slate). The player should be able to read studio health from the air the way a ZT player reads poop piles.

Alert language: subject + place + problem, clickable to jump camera: 'DESERT SERENADE has stalled in Rehearsal - no leading lady (Stage 2)'. Aggregate chorus messages for patterns ('Exhibitors are complaining you have released nothing this quarter') instead of per-entity spam - and throttle hard; GameSpot's ZT2 complaint shows per-entity alerts drown players exactly when they most need guidance.

Escape-equivalent crises should be physical and physically resolved: a star storming off set walks visibly toward the Gate (intercept her - a click on her body - before she leaves the lot); a fire on a stage needs crew to run to it. ZT's escapes work because the emergency and its resolution both live on the map.

Teach the first movie with constrained first choices, not tutorial text: ZT1's starter adoption list is tiny and cheap so the first failure is instant, legible, and recoverable. First session of Project Studio: exactly one screenplay offer, one available director, two actors, one open stage - enough for one B-picture, with the fixer narrating each missing piece. ZT2's 'New Animal Arrivals' pattern also transfers: a first scenario that hands the player three ready pieces (a finished script, a cast, a stage) and asks only that they be matched and greenlit.

Zoopedia transfer: a one-click in-world reference (a trade paper / casting directory card) on every genre, star, and building - what a Western needs, this actor's type and salary, what Soundstage 2 can shoot - readable from any panel BEFORE committing money, so canonical knowledge is not split between advisors and guesswork.

Progression meter on the gate: ZT2's zoo fame stars (which unlock species and objects) map to a studio prestige rating displayed on the studio Gate itself, unlocking genres, bigger stars, and Technicolor - a single always-visible gauge whose growth is the reward schedule.

Anti-lessons: never ship an unexplainable derived number (ZT1's 0-star popularity wall) - every box-office/audience score must decompose on click into named causes; never let advisor text contradict the meters (the camel case); and invest in believable pathing/behavior on the lot, because a world-as-interface game is uniquely damaged when its people visibly behave stupidly (ZT2's trash-can pilgrims).

core_loop: Moment-to-moment: watch the simulated lot run, then left-click-hold to pick up people, scripts, and finished film reels and drop them where they act — a script into the Casting Office's "Begin Casting" room, a star into a role room or next to another star to chat, the completed reel into the Production Office's "Release" room — while tending star moods, repairs, litter, and paving. Session-level: build facilities and shooting sets from the Build menu, recruit wannabes from the physical queue at the Studio Gates, push a stream of five-genre movies through script→cast→shoot→release, climb the Star/Movie/Studio charts, win the five-yearly Lionhead awards, and direct scientists' research (sound, color, CGI, new sets/facilities) across a real-time timeline running from the 1920s to the present. The tycoon loop is deliberately interleaved with an optional auteur loop (Custom Script Office / Advanced Movie Maker / Post Production) where you hand-pick scenes, props, and audio — the seam between those two loops is where the game famously tore.
lot_driven_mechanics: Hiring at the Studio Gates: job-seekers stand in a visible queue outside the front gates (Spacebar centers the camera there). You hire by physically picking a person from the line and dropping them into a role room — e.g. the 'Create Builder' room of the Staff Office, or the actor/director/extra rooms of the Stage School. Hiring is a drag onto a place, never a list transaction.

Building floorplans as verb menus: left-clicking a facility lowers its walls to reveal a labeled floorplan; the rooms ARE the verbs. Casting Office: 'Begin Casting' room plus one room per role; Production Office: Release room, Reviews room, Movie Player room, archive; Script Office: one room per genre (drop a writer into the genre room to commission that genre); Stage School: actor/director/extra rooms plus the 'Import Star' room for StarMaker characters; Staff Office: Create Builder / Create Janitor rooms.

The movie as a physical token: each film is a draggable object mirrored by a HUD Movie Card. You drag the script into 'Begin Casting', drop Stars/extras/crew into the role rooms, then drag the movie icon into the 'Shoot It' room to start photography; the finished reel appears at the Production Office and is dragged into the Release room; dragging the icon onto one of several marketing levels sets the publicity spend; dropping it in the Reviews room first runs a test screening. The card's icon tracks the physical stage: script → movie camera → film can → chart-position number with a pulsing $ while it earns.

Sets as places, not menu entries: sets are constructed on the lot via the Build menu; when shooting starts 'your cast and crew will assemble on set and begin shooting the movie' visibly. A set listed in red in the movie's info bubble means broken / not owned / occupied by another shoot. Idle actors dropped on a set's Rehearse icon gain genre experience. Double-left-click an idle set for a fly-by; double-click an active set to enter a 'director's view' and adjust scene sliders/backdrop while your Stars are filming.

Star care by placement: drop a star next to another star to make them talk (relationships), into the bar/restaurant to de-stress (risking food/drink addiction), into a trailer to assign it, into the rehab facility to cure addiction, onto the Makeover Department (clothes-hanger icon) to re-costume, and drop a staff member next to a star to make them an entourage flunky. Gifts are ornaments physically placed around the star's trailer.

Lot upkeep as a labor loop: builders construct and repair (buildings decay and become unusable until fully repaired); janitors pick up litter and tend grass. Lot prestige factors are all physical: building maintenance, how well-paved the paths between buildings are, litter, toilet/catering capacity relative to head-count on the lot, and quality of ornamentation and flora. Named unattractive items: wide expanses of paving, dead grass, toilet facilities, litter.

Paths and travel time: paving is dragged out slab-by-slab from an existing slab (left-click-hold to extend, right-click-hold to delete). The manual explicitly warns that placing two sets at opposite ends of the lot makes cast and crew 'run back and forth between them, which will extend the production time of your movie... and adding to the movie's cost' — layout is a real economic variable.

Placement grammar: a new building is moved around as a flat ghost footprint, outlined yellow when placement is legal and red when obstructed; hired builders then walk over and construct it in real time (instant-construction is a sandbox toggle). Shift unlocks the ornament cursor from the grid for fine placement.

Photographers as physical agents: as your studio climbs the charts, paparazzi loiter at the gates. You pick one up and hover him near a Star; a camera icon with a tick or cross above the Star shows whether a juicy story exists; dropping him snaps the photo — press rating (and Star rating) up, mood down.
Selling via building: the Star and Script Selling facility works by dropping the star or script you want to sell into the building itself — 'you'll be rewarded with cold, hard cash.'

Attractiveness heatmap: pressing L overlays red/green shading on the ground around buildings; you literally paint red zones green by placing grass, flowerbeds, hedges, and trees, or by placing trash cans and letting a janitor clear the litter.
interaction_grammar: One universal manipulation: left-click-hold picks up any person, script, or movie; release drops it. Left-click a facility shows its floorplan; right-click anything displays all its information bubbles instantly; hovering shows priority-sorted bubbles. Left-click an ornament duplicates it into your hand; right-click gives move options. Nothing can be picked up while paused.

HUD cards are second handles on world objects: Star Cards (portraits, left screen edge) show chart position, mood, and current activity; left-click a card to jump the camera to that person on the lot, click-hold and drag the card to physically pick the person up from wherever they are. Movie Cards (right edge) work the same for films. World and HUD are two views of one draggable entity.

Verbs are discovered by proximity and highlight: hover a held person over a building until the blue floorplan appears, then release into a named room. Yellow/red footprint for building placement, tick/cross over the photographer's target, red set names in the movie bubble — legality is always shown at the drop point.

The Build Button (bottom-left) is the only classic tycoon menu, with three submenus: Facilities ('from toilets to research laboratories'), Sets, and Landscape & Ornaments. Right-clicking an already-built item in the Build menu zooms the camera to it — the menu points back into the world.

Keyboard as teleport map of the production chain: 1 Script Office, 2 Casting Office, 3 Active Set, 4 Production Office, 5 Post Production, 6 Advanced Movie Maker, 7 Staff/Stage School/Crew Office, 8 Sets, 9 Trailers, 0 Research; Tab jumps to the end of the highest-priority guidance stream; F1/F2/F3 open Facilities/Sets/Landscaping; L attractiveness overlay; M overhead map (double-click to travel); Spacebar centers on the Studio Gates.

Camera: free scroll (WASD/arrows/screen-edge push), middle-mouse or Ctrl+arrows to rotate, wheel to zoom, Shift to speed all movement — a fully free orbit camera over a contiguous 3D lot rather than a fixed isometric view.

Time control is part of the grammar: Pause/Play/Fast Forward sit beneath the timeline; you can inspect everything while paused but cannot pick up or drop Stars, staff, movies, or scripts — acting requires time to flow.

The Advanced Movie Maker deliberately 'keeps the same basic drag and drop rules as in the studio' — Stars drag onto lead-role mannequins, costumes drag onto the clothes-hanger icon, scenes drag along a timeline strip, rejects drag to a trash can — so the creative suite reuses the lot's grammar instead of inventing a new one.
attention_language: Information Bubbles: hover (or right-click) any Star, staffer, building, set, or movie card and a stack of bubbles appears, 'intelligently' sorted so the highest-priority information is first. Bubbles contain bars with min/max fills and vertical 'threshold' tick-marks (drop below the lower threshold and performance/happiness visibly suffers). A red '!' bubble means something is really wrong; a blue 'i' bubble is informational. Click a bubble to 'burst' it; clicking the central bubble closes the group.
Pips: small diamond icons that pop on screen as studio status changes — green-backed pip = positive change, red-backed = negative — a constant low-level delta feed alongside the bubbles.

Guiding Streams / Star Trails: the game's flagship teaching device. The moment you pick up a Star, movie, script, or queued person, a sparkling trail draws across the lot from your hand to the most sensible drop target ('this is only a suggestion... you can ignore the guidance'). The same streams appear inside the Build menu, highlighting which icon to select next if the studio lacks something. Tab teleports the camera to the end of the highest-priority stream.

PA System: an in-fiction studio loudspeaker announces problems and developments aloud ('PA Assistance' amount is adjustable in Options; 'Level of Help Provided' separately tunes bubble guidance) — an ambient audio advisor instead of a modal tutor.

The Timeline (top of screen): a scrolling strip of year segments studded with icons for upcoming award ceremonies, research completion dates, real-world events that shift genre popularity, gossip about your Stars, and star retirements (a career-end bubble appears on the timeline with a gold-watch send-off). Hover any icon for details.

In-world body language: Stars' thought bubbles reveal feelings and desires while they chat ('you can gain insight into their feelings and desires by the thought bubbles that appear when two Stars are interacting'); unhappy Stars 'will look unhappy', throw visible tantrums, storm off set to binge at the bar, and ultimately walk out through the gates.

Status iconography on cards: movie cards pulse a $ sign while earning at the box office; the genre icon sits in the card corner; the number on the card is live chart position; star cards show mood and activity at a glance.

Persistent HUD beacons: Studio Ranking rosette (top-right; click for Charts screen), Cash Balance (click for Finance), Awards icon stays lit top-left after each ceremony until reviewed, and the 'i' tutorials button (top-right) hosts per-topic video tutorials.
The L-key attractiveness overlay paints the ground red/green — the lot itself becomes the chart.
first_session_experience: A first New Game cannot skip the in-game interactive tutorial ('Learn the Basics' plus scripted guidance; only on your second new game do you get a skip option). The sequence, per the manual's Quick Start: the camera sits at the Studio Gates where a queue of hopefuls is already standing; you drag one from the line into the Staff Office's Create Builder room (the blue floorplan glow shows the legal drop zone), hire a janitor the same way, then place a Stage School as a yellow/red ghost footprint and watch your builders construct it. You drag gate hopefuls into its actor/director/extra rooms. Critically, 'the in-game tutorial placed a script at the studio gates for you' — your first movie skips the slowest step (scriptwriting) so the first complete loop is cast → shoot → release: drag the free script into the Casting Office's Begin Casting room, drop people into the role rooms exposed by the lowered walls, drag the movie icon into the Shoot It room, watch cast and crew physically walk to the set and film, then drag the finished movie into the Production Office's Release room and drop it on a marketing level. Even ignoring the tutorial, the chain is discoverable because (a) whatever is in your hand emits a sparkling Guiding Stream to the sensible next building, (b) priority-sorted info bubbles and the PA announcer nag about the current blocker, and (c) the movie is a token whose card icon (script → camera → film can) matches where it physically is. Within 15–30 minutes a new player has hired from a visible queue, built one building, and pushed one film through four buildings — the production chain is learned by watching an object travel across the lot, not by reading panels.
criticisms_and_failures: Micromanagement exhaustion was the consensus criticism even in positive reviews: GameSpot (8.2/10) — 'the constant micromanagement can get exhausting' as the same behavioral patterns from talent repeat over decades of game time.

Rock, Paper, Shotgun retrospective (Graham Smith, 2015): the game failed to deliver on its concept — 'the creative suite is limited in terms of what you can make, and the management game splits your time between the fantasy of heading a studio and the tedium of nannying people.'

Relationship grinding via literal re-dragging (Force For Good retrospective): 'you have to force them to talk to each other over and over again on set — and I mean literally, once they've finished a conversation, dragging them back together to talk again, and again, until they develop a friendship' — and it had 'negligible effect on their performances together in movies' while still being required for mogul rankings. The most-cited single tedium in community discussion.

Stars abandoning shoots: stressed/addicted actors 'storm off in the middle of a stressful shoot to stuff their face or chug down some booze,' and the player must chase and re-drag them. Idle Thumbs forum: keeping actors out of the bar between takes was 'one of the biggest ball aches' and made the game 'a chore rather than a pleasure.'

Lot prestige was gameable and unreadable: 'the prestige rating of your lot doesn't seem to be based on anything practical, and you can just mindlessly dot trees around the place until your rating goes up' — decoration became stat-farming (expensive ornament cars) rather than meaningful studio-building.

Artificial staff scarcity as fake difficulty: one limited pool of janitors/crew/extras/scientists/entourage members constantly re-juggled between concurrent productions — bottleneck busywork rather than strategic tradeoff.

No failure drama: 'It's pretty hard to screw things up badly'; you almost never lose money on a film; 'a disastrous shoot that over-runs with numerous disputes between actors and directors... is just never going to happen.' The dominant strategy is crudely 'bigger is better' (more scenes, more actors, longer film), flattening greenlight decisions.

The two-audience split killed it commercially and structurally (Idle Thumbs consensus): bolting a machinima creator onto a tycoon sim 'left you with two average halves' and 'ended up alienating both' audiences. Entering the Advanced Movie Maker 'kills the greedy, money-making momentum' of the tycoon loop; tycoon players resented nannying auteur tools, machinima creators resented the studio grind gating their tools. Creator limits: 3 lead actors per custom script, one primary costume each, preset scenes rather than open tools, set-dressing 'almost impossible to use' (TweakTown), free camera locked behind the Stunts & Effects expansion.

Information overload despite clever prioritization: the screen could become 'totally cluttered with pop-up info bubbles,' and cause-and-effect stayed obtuse — reviewers complained they couldn't tell WHY a movie reviewed badly ('too many limitations and confusion as to why some things work the way they do'). Quality drivers (script age, genre fatigue, star experience mix, set upkeep) were real but opaque.

Late-game repetition: the 1920→present timeline outlasted the systems; once the loop was mastered, decades of identical drag-rituals remained. Edge scored it 7/10, GameSpy 3.5/5 against the 84 Metacritic.

Commercial failure despite critical success: ~50,000 UK copies by end of 2005 (Eurogamer's Kristan Reed: 'relatively minor'), eventually only ELSPA Silver (100k). Molyneux blamed the console shift, the Christmas 2005 release window, and casualization; no sequel was ever made, Lionhead closed in 2016, and Activision delisted the game — the community's repeated verdict is that the concept 'is often imitated but rarely replicated' (Phenixx Gaming 20-year retrospective) and 'deserves a modern sequel.'
